lesson.title: When the Upper Limit Moves: FTC Meets the Chain Rule
lesson.summary: When an accumulation function has a variable upper limit that is itself a function of x, such as g(x), differentiating it correctly requires combining FTC part one with the chain rule, giving F'(x) equal to f(g(x)) times g'(x).
lesson.body:
Every accumulation function so far has had a plain x as its upper limit: F(x) = the integral from a to x of f(t) dt. But what if the upper limit is not x itself, but some function of x, such as x^2? Define F(x) = the integral from a to g(x) of f(t) dt, where g(x) = x^2, or more generally any differentiable function of x. Differentiating F now requires more than FTC part one alone, because F is really a composition of two functions layered on top of each other, and composed functions call for the chain rule.

Here is how the composition works. Let G(u) = the integral from a to u of f(t) dt, an ordinary accumulation function with a plain variable u as its upper limit, so FTC part one applies directly: G'(u) = f(u). Now F(x) = G(g(x)), since accumulating up to g(x) is the same as accumulating up to u and then setting u = g(x). By the chain rule, F'(x) = G'(g(x)) times g'(x), and substituting G'(u) = f(u) gives the general rule: the derivative of the integral from a to g(x) of f(t) dt is f(g(x)) times g'(x). The upper limit gets plugged into f exactly as before, and then, because that upper limit is itself changing at its own rate g'(x), that extra rate of change gets multiplied in.

Here is a fully worked example. Let F(x) = the integral from 0 to x^2 of sin(t) dt, so g(x) = x^2 and g'(x) = 2x. By the rule just derived, F'(x) = sin(g(x)) times g'(x) = sin(x^2) times 2x = 2x sin(x^2). This can be checked directly, since sin(t) does have an elementary antiderivative: an antiderivative of sin(t) is -cos(t), so F(x) = [-cos(t)] from 0 to x^2 = -cos(x^2) - (-cos(0)) = -cos(x^2) + 1 = 1 - cos(x^2). Differentiating this closed form directly, using the chain rule on cos(x^2), gives d/dx[1 - cos(x^2)] = sin(x^2) times 2x = 2x sin(x^2), exactly matching the answer from the shortcut rule.

This combination of FTC part one and the chain rule is what makes accumulation functions flexible enough to handle the variable upper limits that show up constantly in later applications, from probability to physics. It is worth noting, as a brief look ahead, that the same reasoning extends to accumulation functions with a variable lower limit as well, or with both limits varying at once, though the version worked out here, a single moving upper limit combined with the chain rule, covers the core skill you will use most often.
